newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norwegian parties agree 1997 national budget.
newsitem.headline: Norwegian parties agree 1997 national budget.

text.p: Norway's minority Labour government has come to terms with the opposition on the 1997 budget after days of wrangling over how to cover additional spending.

Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg and members of parliament from three centrist opposition parties agreed on Saturday night to allocate an extra five billion crowns ($772.3 million) to local governments.
The opposition thus pushed through its demand that more money be spent on schools and health care, but Stoltenberg said the compromise was reached without upsetting the budget balance.
The extra allocations will be covered mainly through a 3.5 percent rise on alcohol, tobacco and petrol taxes.
The opposition had initially urged the government to chip away at the budget surplus, which is expected to swell to 55.4 billion crowns next year thanks to high oil prices.
"The result is that the balance is unchanged and we have avoided using oil money to finance all kinds of welfare purposes," Stoltenberg told reporters.
"All extra allocations are financed either through cuts in other parts of the budget or through higher taxes," he said. "This means we don't have to risk higher inflation."
Norway produces more than three million barrels per day of oil and is the world's second largest exporter after Saudi Arabia.
But the government has avoided the temptation of going on a spending spree in the draft budget although general elections will be held in September next year.
The final draft presented last month was tight with a strict fiscal policy aimed at restraining price and wage inflation.
The projected budget surplus will be put aside in a state petroleum fund to avoid overheating the economy and to secure pensions for future generations.

Analysts said the battle over the budget had been particularly fierce because an election year is coming up and because the new government of Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland was determined to show strength in the face of a hostile opposition.
Jagland, who is also Labour Party chairman, took over the job as prime minister when veteran Labour premier Gro Harlem Brundtland resigned in October.

The centrist opposition parties -- the Centre Party, the Christian People's Party and liberal Venstre -- saw the budget compromise as a victory for themselves and as a sign that they would be able to co-operate well in the election campaign.
"This shows that the political power lies in the centre and we have emerged as a realistic alternative to the Labour Party," Centre Party parliamentar leader Johan Jakobsen said.
The budget will be formally adopted by parliament this week.
